name: Life-of-mine and annual production plan
summary: Each year the mine's engineers turn the latest mineral reserve into a schedule that shows, year by year until the ore runs out, which tunnels will be driven, which stopes will be mined, how many tonnes and ounces come out and what it will cost. The first year of that schedule, split into months, becomes the production plan behind the company budget and public guidance. Engineering, geology, the superintendents, the site controller, the general manager and the chief operating officer all touch it. It is slow because the schedule is rebuilt by hand in planning software, every change in rates, ventilation limits or gold price forces another pass, and site and head office usually iterate two or three times before the board meets in December.

baseline.org_archetype: A single-mine Canadian gold producer with a 600 tpd underground mine, a technical services team of about 22 at site and an 18-person head office.
baseline.notes: One case is one annual plan cycle from kickoff (late summer) to the issued plan after board approval. A mid-year revision runs a shorter version of the same steps, which is why volume is slightly above one a year.

unit_of_work: one annual life-of-mine plan and production plan
trigger: The corporate budget calendar opens and the latest reserve statement is available as the planning basis.
end_state: The board-approved life-of-mine plan and monthly production plan are issued to short-range planning, finance and disclosure.

volume.seasonality: Work runs from August to December for the budget; a shorter mid-year revision runs in spring after the reserve update.

evidence.note: Annual LOM update (AMC); mid-year revision is the organisation file's assumption.
Four planning engineers; the annual plan and mid-year revision take about 0.4 of one engineer-year, based on the touch time in the steps.
Chief engineer leads the cycle, reviews the schedule and writes capital proposals.
Supplies resource conversion and grade factor assumptions.
Reviews spans and sequence for new mining areas.
Agrees productivity and fleet rates; not listed for this process in the organisation file.
Confirms fleet availability and rebuild schedule; not listed for this process in the organisation file.
Sets throughput and recovery assumptions; not listed for this process in the organisation file.
Builds the site operating cost and headcount model from the physicals; not listed for this process in the organisation file.
Reviews and owns the site plan.
Challenges and accepts the plan for the corporate budget.

systems.name: Mine design and scheduling software (3D design, scheduling)
Shared drives and document library (procedures, permits, drawings)
Mid-market ERP for finance, purchasing, inventory and fixed assets

steps.name: Launch the annual planning cycle
steps.description: The technical services manager opens the corporate budget calendar, the latest published reserve statement and last year's plan, and writes a short planning memo with the deadlines, the reserve model to use and who owns each part. He holds a kickoff meeting with engineering, geology, the superintendents and the site controller.

error.defect_description: Deadlines miss a dependency such as the vent upgrade decision.

evidence.note: The annual LOM review and budget build three to six months before the budget year are described by AMC.

steps.name: Obtain corporate planning assumptions
steps.description: The chief operating officer and head office finance send the gold price, exchange rate, escalation and production targets the site must plan against. The technical services manager chases them by email when the price deck is late, because cut-off grades and stope economics depend on it.

error.defect_description: Price deck differs from the one used in the reserve estimate.

evidence.note: Head office sets the price deck; the reserve estimate used US$1,250/oz at a comparable mine (src3 shows the practice of a long-term price).

steps.name: Load reserve model and depletion into planning software
steps.description: A mine planning engineer imports the reserve block model, the reserve stope shapes and the as-built development and mined-out solids from survey into the mine design and scheduling software. He checks that tonnes and grade in the software match the published reserve tables within rounding.

error.defect_description: Stopes already mined or mis-coded are left in the inventory.

evidence.note: Comparable mine plans in 3D planning software from the reserve model.

steps.name: Set resource conversion and grade factors
steps.description: The chief geologist decides which inferred and target areas may enter the life-of-mine plan beyond reserves, and at what conversion rate, and supplies grade and tonnage factors from the year's mine-to-mill reconciliation. He writes them into a short assumptions table for the engineers.

error.defect_description: Conversion rate is optimistic and inflates later years.

evidence.note: Comparable mine reports LOM schedules with and without resource conversion.

steps.name: Review geotechnical constraints for new areas
steps.description: The geotechnical engineer reviews the planned stoping blocks and sequence for spans, pillar sizes, mining-induced stress and backfill needs, and marks areas that need a centre-out sequence or smaller stopes. He returns a marked-up plan and a list of constraints to the planning engineer.

error.defect_description: A sequence constraint is missed and later forces a schedule change.

evidence.note: Comparable mine adopted a centre-out stoping sequence for stress management. Wait reflects one geotechnical engineer on a two-week rotation.

steps.name: Update development and infrastructure design
steps.description: The planning engineer designs or updates ramps, level accesses, sills, ore and waste passes and ventilation raises needed to reach each stoping block, and classes each metre as operating, capital or exploration development. He records the design in the planning software.

error.defect_description: Development needed to access a block is omitted.

evidence.note: Both comparable plans split development into operating and capital metres.

steps.name: Check ventilation and services capacity
steps.description: The planning engineer checks the airflow available on each level against the diesel fleet the schedule needs, and the hoisting, pumping and backfill capacity, and flags years where a fan, raise or upgrade must be in place first. Ventilation limits are the most common reason the planned mining rate has to be cut.

error.defect_description: Fleet in the schedule exceeds available air in some months.

evidence.note: The reference mine's 600 tpd target depended on a ventilation upgrade.

steps.name: Agree productivity and fleet rates
steps.description: The planning engineer meets the mine superintendent and maintenance superintendent to agree development advance per heading, stope cycle times, equipment availability and the rebuild schedule. They compare the rates with last year's actuals from shift reports before accepting them.

error.defect_description: Rates are set from targets rather than actuals and are too high.

evidence.note: Superintendents on 14/14 rotation; the wait is for both to be on site. Practice from general knowledge of underground scheduling.

steps.name: Build the life-of-mine schedule
steps.description: The planning engineer schedules every development heading and stope year by year and month by month for the first two years, levelling the work to the number of jumbos, bolters, loaders, trucks and the hoist. He iterates the sequence until tonnes and grade are smooth and the backfill cycle is met.

error.defect_description: Sequence conflicts or unrealistic ramp-up in the schedule.

evidence.note: AMC describes scheduling mining and treatment operations and generating mine designs within the planning cycle.

steps.name: Set mill throughput and recovery plan
steps.description: The mill superintendent reviews the monthly ore tonnes and head grade from the draft schedule, sets mill throughput, planned shutdown days and recovery by ore source, and returns the processing plan. He flags months where ore supply is below the mill's economic rate.

error.defect_description: Recovery assumption not updated for a new ore source.

evidence.note: Mill plan follows the mine schedule; recovery of about 97 percent at the reference mill (organisation file).

steps.name: Convert physicals into cost drivers
steps.description: The planning engineer exports metres, tonnes, equipment hours, backfill volumes and consumables by year into the cost workbook in the format the site controller uses. He lists capital items such as raises, fans and fleet replacements with their timing.

error.defect_description: Units or periods are mis-keyed between the planning software and the workbook.

evidence.note: Budget physical quantities drive budget costs through cost models (AMC).

steps.name: Build operating cost and headcount model
steps.description: The site controller applies unit costs, labour rates, contractor rates and headcount to the physicals and produces operating cost per tonne, cost per ounce and the capital estimate by year. He compares the result with the year's forecast and asks engineering to explain large differences.

error.defect_description: Labour or contractor rates out of date.

evidence.note: Site controller owns cost models at a single-mine producer; costs per tonne at comparable mines in the organisation file.

steps.name: Technical review of schedule and costs
steps.description: The technical services manager reviews the schedule against the reserve, the rates and the capacity limits, checks year-one physicals against the current year's actuals, and lists corrections. About a third of drafts go back for rescheduling.

error.defect_description: Review misses an error that surfaces at head office.

control.basis: Company planning procedure: chief engineer review before site sign-off

evidence.note: Rework share from general practice; the manager is on rotation so reviews wait for him.

steps.name: Draft capital project proposals
steps.description: The technical services manager writes a proposal for each major capital item in the plan, such as a ventilation raise, a fan upgrade or a fleet addition, with cost, timing, alternatives and the production at risk without it. He sends them with the plan for capital approval.

error.defect_description: Proposal cost estimate omits indirects.

evidence.note: Reference mine split 2021 capital into sustaining and growth items.

steps.name: Site management review
steps.description: The general manager walks through the plan with the superintendents, site controller and technical services manager, challenges rates and costs and decides what the site will commit to. About a quarter of plans go back for changes to rates or sequence.

error.defect_description: Commitment made to a target the schedule cannot support.

control.basis: Delegation of authority: site plan endorsed by the general manager

evidence.note: Site review meeting typical of TSX producers; share of plans sent back is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Run price and cost scenarios
steps.description: The planning engineer and site controller run the plan at the low and high gold price and cost cases, and with and without the conversion tonnes, to give head office the guidance range. They summarise ounces, cost per ounce and capital for each case in one table.

error.defect_description: Scenario uses a stale cost model.

evidence.note: Comparable mine shows LOM NPV sensitivity to gold price and grade.

steps.name: Present plan to head office
steps.description: The general manager sends the plan, scenario table and capital proposals to the chief operating officer and chief financial officer and presents them at a planning meeting, usually by video call from site. He records the questions raised.

error.defect_description: Presentation figures differ from the workbook.

evidence.note: Head office review meeting before the budget goes to the board.

steps.name: Head office challenge and acceptance
steps.description: The chief operating officer reviews the plan against guidance, corporate cash needs and analyst expectations, and either accepts it or asks for more ounces, lower costs or deferred capital. About a third of plans need another scheduling pass.

error.defect_description: A requested change is not carried into the schedule.

control.basis: Corporate budget process: COO acceptance of the site plan

evidence.note: Iteration between site and head office is common; shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Produce the monthly production plan for the budget
steps.description: The planning engineer splits year one into months with tonnes, grade, ounces, development metres, backfill and stopes by level, and checks the months against planned mill shutdowns and holidays. He passes the file to head office finance for the budget.

error.defect_description: Monthly phasing ignores a planned shutdown.

evidence.note: The budget is the year-one slice of the rolling plan (AMC).

steps.name: Wait for board approval of budget and guidance
steps.description: Head office takes the plan into the budget package and the board of directors considers it at its December meeting; the site waits for the decision. In a minority of years the board asks for changes that send the plan back for scenarios.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

control.basis: Board approval of the annual budget under the company's governance mandate

evidence.note: Reference company issued annual guidance in mid-January, after the board cycle.

steps.name: Finalise and issue the plan documents
steps.description: The technical services manager updates the plan for any final changes, writes the life-of-mine plan report and issues it with the schedule files to short-range planning, finance and the disclosure team. He records the version in the document library.

error.defect_description: Superseded schedule version issued.

evidence.note: Plan report and file handover typical of site practice.

steps.name: Hand over to short-range planning
steps.description: The planning engineer walks the short-range planners through the first-year sequence, the key constraints and the capital timing so the monthly plans start from the approved plan. He archives the planning database for next year's cycle.

error.defect_description: A constraint is not passed on.

evidence.note: Handover practice from general knowledge.

steps.name: Revise schedule and costs for review comments
steps.description: The planning engineer works through the reviewer's list: resequences stopes, changes rates or capital timing, reruns the schedule for the affected years and refreshes the physicals export for the cost model. He sends the revised version back for technical review with a list of what changed.

error.defect_description: A change made for one comment breaks another part of the sequence.

evidence.note: Partial rescheduling pass; effort is the author's estimate at about a fifth of the first build.

exceptions.name: Rescheduling after technical review
exceptions.description: The chief engineer finds sequence conflicts, missed development or rates above actuals and sends the schedule back.

exceptions.name: Head office asks for more ounces or less capital
exceptions.description: The COO returns the plan for new scenarios or a new schedule to meet guidance or cash targets.

exceptions.name: Board requests changes
exceptions.description: The board asks for a lower-risk case or deferred capital and the plan is rerun before guidance.

exceptions.name: Ventilation limit cuts the mining rate
exceptions.description: The capacity check shows the fleet needs more air than available until an upgrade is built, and the schedule and capital timing are rebuilt.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from kickoff to issued plan
benchmarks.population: Annual plan cycle at a single-mine underground producer

evidence.note: AMC says the budget-year plan is created three to six months before the year starts; the author places the median at about 15 weeks including board approval.

benchmarks.population: Reference mine (Eagle River) after ventilation upgrade

pain_points.description: Each change to rates, price or ventilation forces the schedule to be rebuilt by hand in the planning software, so most of the cycle is rework loops between s09 and the reviews.

evidence.note: Rework shares in the steps; general knowledge of manual scheduling.

pain_points.description: Physicals are re-keyed from the planning software into the finance workbook, and unit or period errors show up only when costs look wrong.

evidence.note: Budget physicals drive cost models (AMC); re-keying is the author's assumption for 2019-2022 tools.

pain_points.description: Reviewers on two-week rotations hold the work while they are off site.

evidence.note: 14/14 rotations in the organisation file.

pain_points.description: Ventilation capacity rather than ore availability often caps the plan, and the fix is a capital project with its own lead time.

evidence.note: The reference mine's higher mining rate waited for a ventilation upgrade.

sources.title: Long-term mine planning and the mine-planning process
sources.supports: Planning hierarchy: life-of-mine plan reviewed and updated annually, five-year plan generated annually, two-year rolling plan updated quarterly, annual budget taken from the plan version created three to six months before the budget year; budget physical quantities drive costs through cost models; planning covers geological and geotechnical inputs, mine designs, mining and treatment schedules and cash flow forecasts; failing to look far enough ahead is a common cause of operational problems

sources.supports: Comparable Ontario mine: life-of-mine schedules with and without resource conversion (Table 15-2 and 15-3), 3D planning software, development split into operating and capital metres, LOM cash flow and NPV sensitivity to gold price and grade; ventilation and hoisting capacity as constraints on the plan

assumptions: Loaded costs come from the organisation file (salary times 1.30 for staff roles).

The simulated median of about 128 days is about three weeks longer than the 105-day benchmark. The simulator adds the roughly 620 hands-on hours to elapsed time as if one person worked them back to back, around the clock; in practice two or three engineers work the design, schedule and cost model in parallel during day shifts, which roughly cancels out. The simulated p90 (about 185 days) is above the benchmark p90 because a plan that loops through head office and board changes twice would in practice be cut short by the December board date and finished as a mid-year revision.
The planning software is a commercial 3D design and scheduling package; the product name is not stated because the reference mine's choice was not confirmed.
Mine superintendent, maintenance superintendent, mill superintendent and site controller take part but are not listed for this process in the organisation file's process map.
The board approval step is shown as a calendar wait because board decisions are handled by the corporate budget process.
